nameStory: The 'sea slater' gets its name from its resemblance to terrestrial slaters (another name for pill bugs or roly-polies), but this one lives by the sea. The word 'slater' comes from the old belief that these creatures could split or 'slate' rocks with their powerful legs. Some folks also call them 'sea roaches' due to their quick, scurrying movements across wet rocks.
description: The Common Sea Slater is a marine cousin of the familiar pill bug, but much larger and exclusively coastal. These oval, flattened creatures can grow up to about 1.4 inches long, making them giants among their terrestrial relatives. They have segmented, armor-like bodies with seven pairs of legs and long, prominent antennae. Their gray to brownish coloration helps them blend perfectly with wet rocks and seaweed.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Remarkably large for an isopod, reaching up to 1.4 inches long - about the size of your thumb from tip to first joint

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval and flattened like a pill bug that's been gently pressed down, with distinct segmentation across the back

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, conspicuous antennae that are constantly twitching and exploring - much longer than a pill bug's

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled gray to brownish, often with a slight greenish tinge when wet, perfectly matching barnacle-crusted rocks

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Incredibly fast and agile, scurrying across rocks with surprising speed when disturbed - much quicker than terrestrial isopods

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of walking legs that grip wet, slippery surfaces with remarkable tenacity

habitat: Look for Common Sea Slaters in the splash zone of rocky coastlines, particularly around tide pools and barnacle-covered boulders. They hide in crevices, under seaweed, and beneath rocks during low tide, emerging when waves splash over their hiding spots. They're most common on exposed Atlantic shores with plenty of rocky surfaces and good wave action.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, often seen scurrying across rocks during spring tides when wave action increases their activity.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easily spotted during warm summer days, especially in early morning or evening when they venture further from cracks and crevices.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may retreat deeper into rock crevices as temperatures drop and storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Less active but still present; look for them on warmer days when waves splash their hiding spots, though they'll be slower moving.

funFact: Sea slaters are actually living barometers - they become noticeably more active and venture further from their hiding spots when atmospheric pressure drops before storms, as if they can sense the approaching rough seas that will bring them food and moisture.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with terrestrial pill bugs or sow bugs that wash up on beaches, but sea slaters are dramatically larger and have much longer antennae. Remember: if it's huge for a 'roly-poly' and has antennae like whiskers, it's a sea slater.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'slaters' like their terrestrial cousins, sea slaters cannot roll into a ball like pill bugs can. This ability was lost as they adapted to life in the harsh marine environment where speed and strong grip matter more than armor.
compareHints: The Common Sea Slater is distinguished from its relative the Wharf Louse by its larger size and preference for natural rocky shores rather than harbors and docks. Common Sea Slaters are also more uniformly gray-brown, while Wharf Lice tend to have more mottled patterns and prefer the calmer waters of protected harbors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The wharf louse is extremely similar to its close relative, the common sea slater, and telling them apart requires close examination of small anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field.
